newsitem.title: IRAN: U.S. holds key to relations with Iran - Khatami.
newsitem.headline: U.S. holds key to relations with Iran - Khatami.

text.p: The United States, not the Islamic republic, holds the key to breaking the ice in relations with Iran, incoming Iranian president Mohammad Khatami said on Tuesday.

"Our relations with the United States will depend on observing changes in their attitude towards us, but unfortunately we have not seen anything," he said at his first news conference since a landslide election victory on Friday.
"Therefore, the key of the problem is in their hands and not ours," he said through an interpreter.

Khatami, a moderate whose election was Iran's biggest political upset since Shi'ite Moslem fundamentalists ousted the U.S.-backed Shah in 1979, is due to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani in August.
He said: "We are sorry to see that the United States' policy has always been hostile to our revolution."
Iran and the United States have had no diplomatic relations since 1980 at the height of the U.S. embassy crisis in Iran when radicals held 52 Americans captive for 444 days.
Although Khatami is a moderate Shi'ite Moslem clergyman compared with the conservative clerics who control the Iranian establishment, the tone of his remarks was uncompromising.
He said the United States was the source of the problem of relations and there would be no ground for any ties as long as the United States wanted to harm Iranian independence or national interest.
"The great outcome of our revolution is independence and we are not willing to give up this valuable outcome we have gained," he said.
"The basis of our relations with other countries relies on the independence and national interest of our country."

U.S. analysts in Washington on Monday described Khatami's election as a turning point in the revolution and said the Clinton administration should rethink its policy of isolating the Islamic republic.
The seizure of the U.S. hostages in 1979 poisoned relations between Tehran and Washington, previously close while the pro-American Shah was in power.

The two former allies have been in a state of declared enmity ever since with the United States accusing Iran of sponsoring international "terrorism", seeking nuclear arms and trying to wreck Middle East peace efforts.
Khatami dismissed charges of Iranian involvement in international "terrorism", saying: "We have always been against terrorism and especially state terrorism."
In 1988 a U.S. cruiser shot down an Iranian airliner over the Gulf, killing all 290 aboard. Washington said it was a mistake.
After President Bill Clinton took office in 1993 he launched a drive to isolate Iran.
The Washington analysts said the United States should respond with new overtures to show it was serious about its oft- stated readiness to open a new dialogue.
